amazing-grace.text: These words were first printed in 1779, in Olney Hymns, a hymnbook made in an English village with the poet William Cowper. Their title there was Faith's Review and Expectation.
The tune uses only five different notes, a pentatonic scale. Moved to F sharp major, all five are black keys on a piano.
amazing-grace.source: The tune's own notes (G, A, B, D and E)

amazing-grace.text: The tune, now called New Britain, was printed in 1829 in Columbian Harmony, a shape-note book whose notes have shapes that show their place in the scale.

The verse about ten thousand years, often sung last, isn't Newton's: it grew from a Philadelphia hymn of the 1780s and took today's words in a Virginia collection of 1790. Harriet Beecher Stowe printed it with Amazing Grace in Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852), and no hymnal is known to pair them before 1909.

happy-birthday.text: The tune began as Good Morning to All, a morning greeting for a kindergarten class, by the sisters Mildred and Patty Hill. Its earliest known printing is in their Song Stories for the Kindergarten, published in 1893.
happy-birthday.source: US District Court, Central District of California, No. CV 13-4460-GHK (MRWx), order of 22 September 2015, pp. 1-2; and IMSLP, Happy Birthday to You (Hill, Mildred)

happy-birthday.text: For decades a music publisher, lately Warner/Chappell, charged fees to use the song in films and on television. On 22 September 2015 the US District Court for the Central District of California ruled that Warner/Chappell did not own a valid copyright in the words.
happy-birthday.source: US District Court, Central District of California, No. CV 13-4460-GHK (MRWx), order of 22 September 2015, conclusion, p. 43; and Berkeley Technology Law Journal, "The original happy song: now free for all" (December 2015)

happy-birthday.text: In the European Union, any copyright in the song ran out at the end of 2016, seventy years after Patty Hill died in 1946.
happy-birthday.source: Musicalities Ltd (UK music copyright consultancy), "Do I have to pay to record Happy Birthday?"; and Stephen Carlisle, "Happy Birthday is in the public domain?", Nova Southeastern University (2015)

happy-birthday.text: The 1998 Guinness Book of World Records named it the most recognised song in the English language.
happy-birthday.source: Renee C. Quinn and Brian Focarino, IPWatchdog (28 October 2015); and Joyce Klemmer, Smith Gambrell & Russell, "The Happy Birthday song: how old are you now?" (Mondaq / Legal 500, 16 September 2015)

michael-row.text: In 1961 a folk group of five Wesleyan University students took the song, under the title "Michael", to number one in the United States and in Britain.
michael-row.source: Wesleyan University, History and Traditions (trivia); Official Charts Company, "Michael" (1961); number1sblog (UK number ones); Associated Press obituary of Dave Fisher (2010)

michael-row.text: The Michael of the song is usually taken to be the archangel Michael.
michael-row.source: William Francis Allen, introduction to Slave Songs of the United States (New York: A. Simpson, 1867), p. xvi; Jeff Place, notes to Pete Seeger: The Smithsonian Folkways Collection (SFW 40225, 2019), p. 61

are-you-sleeping.text: In the French words the sleeping brother is supposed to ring the bell for matins, the church's prayers said at night; the last line, "din, din, don", is that bell.
are-you-sleeping.source: Charles-Marie Widor, Vieilles chansons pour les petits enfants (Paris, 1883), pp. 18-19, read from the scan; and Fernand Cabrol, "Matins", The Catholic Encyclopedia, vol. 10 (1911)

are-you-sleeping.text: The tune's earliest known printing, Paris 1811, has no words at all: it is air No. 726 in La Clé du Caveau, a book of song tunes, listed as the air of Brother Jacques's matins.
are-you-sleeping.source: La Clé du Caveau (Paris: Capelle et Renand, 1811), air No. 726, p. 309, and its table, read from the scan

silent-night.text: Mohr asked Gruber for music for two solo voices and choir, with guitar, and the carol was first sung that way that same night, Christmas Eve 1818.
Mohr wrote six verses. The English most people sing, John Freeman Young's from 1859, is based on just three of them: the first, the sixth and the second.
Its earliest known printing with music, around 1833 in Dresden, was among four 'genuine Tyrolean songs' sung by the Strassers, a travelling family of singers who also made gloves.

Gruber wrote his tune in 6/8 time, a simple lullaby in the rhythm of a siciliana. The melody sung today differs slightly from his, most of all at the first "Sleep in heavenly peace", which begins a third higher.
silent-night.source: Psalter Hymnal Handbook (1998), STILLE NACHT, at Hymnary.org, and Gottfried Kasparek, "Stille Nacht: a scientific view", SalzburgerLand

auld-lang-syne.text: Burns's words were first printed in 1796 to a slow, haunting tune. The tune we sing joined them in 1799, in George Thomson's collection of Scottish airs.
auld-lang-syne.source: The Conversation (Kirsteen McCue, University of Glasgow), "How Auld Lang Syne switched tunes en route to world domination"

auld-lang-syne.text: In Scotland, the singers stand in a circle holding hands, and cross their arms, still holding hands, only as the last verse begins, not from the first line.
auld-lang-syne.source: Scotland.org (Scottish Government), "The history and words of Auld Lang Syne"; and VisitEdinburgh (edinburgh.org), "Have a traditional New Year in Edinburgh"

auld-lang-syne.text: Burns said the song was old and had never been printed or even written down until he took it down from an old man's singing.
auld-lang-syne.source: Library of Congress, Folklife Today, "Auld Acquaintance for the New Year: Burns's Auld Lang Syne"

auld-lang-syne.text: Burns didn't begin from nothing: several lines of his earliest version match an older song printed in 1711, in James Watson's Choice Collection of Scots Poems.
auld-lang-syne.source: Library of Congress, Folklife Today, "Auld Acquaintance for the New Year: Burns's Auld Lang Syne"

auld-lang-syne.text: In Japan the tune carries other words, Hotaru no Hikari, whose earliest known printing is in a government school songbook dated 1881. Shops play it at closing time to see customers out.
auld-lang-syne.source: Shogaku shokashu, shohen (Ministry of Education), colophon dated 24 November 1881, Tokyo Gakugei University archive record; and Ikeda Sayuri, Meiji songbook notes (No. 20 "Hotaru"); closing time: The World (PRI, 2015) and SoraNews24 (2024)

be-thou-my-vision.text: The Irish poem is sometimes credited to a saint of the 500s, but its language points to the 10th or 11th century. Its oldest surviving copies date from the 1400s or 1500s.
The tune is an Irish folk melody. In Patrick Joyce's 1909 collection of old Irish folk music it went with a love song, With My Love on the Road.
A hymnal handbook praises the tune's wide-ranging phrases, and says its usual harmony suits good singers, especially low basses.
be-thou-my-vision.source: Hymnary.org, "SLANE" (tune notes from the Psalter Hymnal Handbook, 1988)

be-thou-my-vision.text: The same tune carries another hymn, Lord of All Hopefulness, first printed with it in 1931. Its writer, Jan Struther, is best known in England for her novel Mrs Miniver.
be-thou-my-vision.source: Hymnary.org, "Lord of all hopefulness, Lord of all joy"

shenandoah.text: At sea it became a capstan shanty: sailors sang it while turning the capstan, a big upright winch, to haul in the anchor.
shenandoah.source: Richard Runciman Terry, The Shanty Book, Part I (London: Curwen, 1921), introduction p. vii and No. 9, "Shenandoah (Windlass and Capstan)"; Stephen Winick, "A Deep Dive Into Sea Shanties", Library of Congress Folklife Today (2021)

shenandoah.text: In some old versions Shenandoah is a man, not a river: a Native American chief, whose daughter a trader falls in love with.
shenandoah.source: W. B. Whall, Ships, Sea Songs and Shanties (3rd ed., Glasgow: Brown, Son & Ferguson, 1913), pp. 1 to 3; Richard Runciman Terry, The Shanty Book, Part I (1921), note to No. 9

shenandoah.text: The shanty collector Richard Runciman Terry wrote that every sailor he met knew it, yet no two sang it quite alike, and that it was always sung with deep feeling, in a very free rhythm.
shenandoah.source: Mainly Norfolk, "Shenandoah" (Martyn Wyndham-Read song notes, quoting Terry)

o-come-all-ye-faithful.text: John Francis Wade earned his living copying and selling plainchant and other music by hand. The hymn survives in several manuscripts he signed.
In London it caught on at the Portuguese embassy chapel, where Samuel Webbe was organist. Sheet music of about 1799 sold it as the favourite Portuguese hymn.
Frederick Oakeley's English version of about 1841 began with a different line. The opening everyone sings now came from a reworking in an 1852 hymnal.
The Latin hymn grew to eight verses: Wade's four, three by Borderies printed in 1822, and an anonymous one in print by 1857. An 1884 hymnal made the first real try at all eight in English.

ode-to-joy.text: Beethoven's own tune pushes in early, with an accent just before the last phrase. Many hymnals, and our arrangement, square that line up on the beat.
ode-to-joy.source: Hymnology Archive, "Joyful, Joyful, We Adore Thee"; and Hymnal for American Youth, ed. H. Augustine Smith (New York: The Century Co., 1919), No. 47, p. 38, read from the scan

ode-to-joy.text: On Christmas Day 1989, weeks after the Berlin Wall opened, Leonard Bernstein conducted it in Berlin with players from Dresden, Leningrad, London, New York and Paris, the chorus singing Freiheit (freedom) for Freude (joy).
ode-to-joy.source: Leonard Bernstein Office, "Berlin Wall (1989)", Historic Concerts

ode-to-joy.text: Schiller wrote the poem in 1785, and it appeared the next year in his magazine Thalia. Beethoven's sung text isn't all Schiller: its first lines, "O Freunde, nicht diese Töne", are Beethoven's own.
ode-to-joy.source: Simon Chlosta, "Beethoven 9: Musical world cultural heritage", Elbphilharmonie Mediatheque (2022); Thalia, vol. 1, no. 2 (Leipzig: Göschen, 1786), pp. 1 to 5, as given by Bibliotheca Augustana; Peter Laki, programme note, The Cleveland Orchestra

ode-to-joy.text: In a 1907 letter, Henry van Dyke said he wrote these words with Beethoven's music always in his head, and gave the melody the credit for whatever was good in them.
ode-to-joy.source: Hymnology Archive, "Joyful, Joyful, We Adore Thee"

ode-to-joy.text: In 1846 Elam Ives printed the melody as a hymn tune called Bonn, adding a pickup note before every phrase to fit the words.
ode-to-joy.source: Hymnology Archive, "Joyful, Joyful, We Adore Thee"

row-row-row.text: Today's tune appears in the Franklin Square Song Collection of 1881, a songbook for schools and homes, printed as a round and credited to E. O. Lyte.
row-row-row.source: J. P. McCaskey, Franklin Square Song Collection (New York: Harper & Brothers, 1881), p. 69, "Row Your Boat. (Round.)", E. O. Lyte; preface: "for the People at large, in their Homes and Schools"

row-row-row.text: Leave out the quick passing notes and every note of the tune belongs to one chord, the home chord. That's why it makes such an easy round: any voice fits any other.
row-row-row.source: J. P. McCaskey, Franklin Square Song Collection (New York: Harper & Brothers, 1881), p. 69, "Row Your Boat (Round)", E. O. Lyte; Beth's Notes, "Row, Row, Row Your Boat" (music-teaching resource, 2013): "Harmony: one chord"

shchedryk.text: Shchedryk is built on an ostinato: one short four-note figure that keeps repeating while the other voices build around it.
shchedryk.source: America Magazine (Jim McDermott, 2022), "The story of 'Carol of the Bells,' a Christmas classic born in Ukraine"

shchedryk.text: In Shchedryk's Ukrainian words, a swallow flies into a household and tells the family how rich their coming year will be.
shchedryk.source: The song's own words (a shchedrivka, a New Year's well-wishing song); Interlude, "Carol of the Bells by Mykola Leontovych: History and Recordings"

shchedryk.text: The same chorus sang Shchedryk at Carnegie Hall on 5 October 1922, its first performance in the United States.
shchedryk.source: America Magazine (Jim McDermott, 2022), "The story of 'Carol of the Bells,' a Christmas classic born in Ukraine"

shchedryk.text: Oleksander Koshyts's Ukrainian National Chorus carried Shchedryk abroad, giving hundreds of concerts in 45 cities across 10 European countries in two years.
shchedryk.source: America Magazine (Jim McDermott, 2022), "The story of 'Carol of the Bells,' a Christmas classic born in Ukraine"

shchedryk.text: Shchedryk is one of more than 150 choral pieces Leontovych made from Ukrainian folk songs, and by far the best known.
shchedryk.source: Encyclopedia of Ukraine (Canadian Institute of Ukrainian Studies), "Leontovych, Mykola"

simple-gifts.text: Shaker manuscripts also call it Dancing Song or Quick Dance. It was meant to go fast, and the words of its second half, about bowing, bending and turning, were dance directions.
simple-gifts.source: American Music Preservation (Roger Lee Hall), "Joseph Brackett's 'Simple Gifts': Shaker simplicity in song"

simple-gifts.text: Sydney Carter's 1963 hymn Lord of the Dance is sung to this tune, so hymnals print the melody with his words as well as the original Shaker ones.
simple-gifts.source: Hymnary.org, "Lord of the Dance" (text) and "SIMPLE GIFTS" (tune)

simple-gifts.text: In 1950 Copland also arranged it for voice and piano, in his first set of Old American Songs. Peter Pears and Benjamin Britten gave the first performance, at Aldeburgh in England.
simple-gifts.source: IRCAM, Brahms database, "Old American Songs I (1950)"

swing-low.text: The melody is pentatonic, made from just five notes, and built for call and response: a soloist sings the verses while the group answers with the repeated lines.
swing-low.source: Hymnology Archive (Chris Fenner), "Swing Low, Sweet Chariot"

swing-low.text: The oldest known recording of it is a wax cylinder made in 1894 by the Standard Quartette, an African American vocal group.
An 1874 book, Hampton and Its Students, printed it with a very different melody, one that is also pentatonic.
swing-low.source: Hymnology Archive (Chris Fenner), "Swing Low, Sweet Chariot"

swing-low.text: In 1917 Harry T. Burleigh arranged it as a concert song for solo voice and piano, published by G. Ricordi.
swing-low.source: Hymnology Archive (Chris Fenner), "Swing Low, Sweet Chariot"

swing-low.text: In 2011 Oklahoma made it the state's official gospel song.
swing-low.source: State Symbols USA, "Oklahoma State Gospel Song: 'Swing Low, Sweet Chariot' by Wallis Willis"

red-river-valley.text: The oldest known written copy of the words is a manuscript found in Iowa, marked with the year 1879.
red-river-valley.source: Manitoba Historical Society, Manitoba History no. 72 (2013), James J. Nystrom, "The True Story of the Song 'Red River Valley'"

red-river-valley.text: Carl T. Sprague recorded it in 1925 under another name, Cowboy Love Song. A 1927 record by Hugh Cross and Riley Puckett became the cowboy version's biggest hit.
red-river-valley.source: Manitoba Historical Society, Manitoba History no. 72 (2013), James J. Nystrom, "The True Story of the Song 'Red River Valley'"

red-river-valley.text: The folklorist Edith Fowke called it probably the best known folk song on the Canadian prairies.
red-river-valley.source: Manitoba Historical Society, Manitoba History no. 72 (2013), James J. Nystrom, "The True Story of the Song 'Red River Valley'"

red-river-valley.text: It is the official slow march of the Fort Garry Horse, a Canadian Army regiment based in Winnipeg.
red-river-valley.source: Government of Canada, National Defence, "The Fort Garry Horse" (official lineage)

red-river-valley.text: Red River Valley is heard in John Ford's 1940 film of The Grapes of Wrath.
red-river-valley.source: Film Forum, "The Grapes of Wrath" (program note)

home-on-the-range.text: In 1908 the folk song collector John Lomax recorded a saloon keeper singing it, a man who had once driven cattle up the Chisholm Trail.
home-on-the-range.source: Kansas Historical Society, Kansapedia, "Home on the Range"

home-on-the-range.text: In 1934 an Arizona couple sued for $500,000, saying it copied their own song, My Arizona Home. Their claim was rejected.
home-on-the-range.source: Kansas Historical Society, Kansapedia, "Home on the Range"

home-on-the-range.text: In 1933 President Franklin D. Roosevelt named it his favorite song.
home-on-the-range.source: Kansas Historical Society, Kansapedia, "Home on the Range"

all-through-the-night.text: It was first printed in 1784, in Edward Jones's Musical and Poetical Relicks of the Welsh Bards, as a song for voice and harp with five variations on the accompaniment.
all-through-the-night.source: Hymnology Archive, "God That Madest Earth and Heaven" (AR HYD Y NOS)

all-through-the-night.text: Hymnals list its metre as 8.4.8.4.8.8.8.4: long lines answered by a short one. In the English song that short line is the title, and it waits out three long lines before closing.
all-through-the-night.source: Hymnary.org, "AR HYD Y NOS" (tune information); Wikisource, "Ar Hyd y Nos (Boulton/Maynard)"

all-through-the-night.text: An 1881 account says Reginald Heber wrote his evening hymn, God That Madest Earth and Heaven, after hearing this air played on a harp at a country house in Wales.
all-through-the-night.source: Hymnology Archive, "God That Madest Earth and Heaven"

all-through-the-night.text: A Dublin schoolbook named this air for Heber's evening hymn by 1838, yet hymnbooks long kept the two apart. One hymn scholar called the English Hymnal's pairing of 1906 one of its boldest strokes.
all-through-the-night.source: Hymnology Archive, "God That Madest Earth and Heaven" (quoting Erik Routley on the English Hymnal's "boldest strokes"); and Sacred Poetry: Adapted to the Understanding of Children and Youth (Dublin: Commissioners of National Education, 1838), p. 16, No. XI, "Evening Hymn", to the air "Ar hydd y-nos", read from the scan

blow-the-man-down.text: It's a halyard shanty, for hoisting heavy yards. The crew rested on the rope while the shantyman sang his line, then took a big pull together as they roared the refrain.
blow-the-man-down.source: Mainly Norfolk, "Blow the Man Down" (A.L. Lloyd songs; Topic Records sleeve notes)

blow-the-man-down.text: The Traditional Ballad Index gives its earliest known date as July 1867, in a Syracuse newspaper, the Daily Courier.
blow-the-man-down.source: The Traditional Ballad Index (California State University, Fresno), "Blow the Man Down"

blow-the-man-down.text: The shanty collector Stan Hugill sorted the song into six separate versions, among them the Flash Packet, the Blackballer and the Milkmaid.
blow-the-man-down.source: The Traditional Ballad Index, "Blow the Man Down", notes

blow-the-man-down.text: The same tune, with other words, turned up as Roll 'Im On Down, a song for launching boats, recorded in 1935.
blow-the-man-down.source: The Traditional Ballad Index, "Blow the Man Down", Same Tune and notes

danny-boy.text: Jane Ross of Limavady, who collected the tune, could say only that it was very old.
danny-boy.source: Minerva Classics, "A Source Guide to the Music of Percy Grainger" (Irish Tune from County Derry), quoting Petrie

danny-boy.text: The melody saves its peak for the second half: from the halfway mark it climbs to its highest notes.
danny-boy.source: The Methodist Church in Britain, "I cannot tell why he, whom angels worship (StF 350)", notes on the tune

danny-boy.text: How old is the tune? Some 20th-century writers suspected its collector shaped it herself, but a 2000 study argued it really is old, and was shaped by tradition.
danny-boy.source: Brian Audley, "The Provenance of the Londonderry Air", Journal of the Royal Musical Association 125:2 (2000), abstract, Cambridge Core

danny-boy.text: Percy Grainger set the tune for unaccompanied voices in October 1902, as Irish Tune from County Derry, and later made versions for instruments and band.
danny-boy.source: Minerva Classics, "A Source Guide to the Music of Percy Grainger", Irish Tune from County Derry

danny-boy.text: Churches sing the same tune to a hymn, I Cannot Tell, by William Young Fullerton, who grew up in Ireland and became a Baptist minister.
danny-boy.source: The Methodist Church in Britain, "I cannot tell why he, whom angels worship (StF 350)"

loch-lomond.text: Its earliest known printing is a song sheet, Bonnie Loch Loman, published in Edinburgh by Paterson & Roy in about 1840, its seven verses "written by a lady". The tune is probably older, from an old Scottish air.
loch-lomond.source: Brown's Book-Stall, No. 75 (Aberdeen, December 1911), pp. 5 and 7, quoting Gavin Greig and reprinting the sheet's words; Alfred Moffat, The Minstrelsy of Scotland (Augener), p. 34, note (the air from "Kind Robin lo'es me", printed 1742)

loch-lomond.text: Ralph Vaughan Williams arranged it in 1921 for unaccompanied choir, and his setting has become a famous one.
loch-lomond.source: Classical-Music.com (BBC Music Magazine's website), "Loch Lomond lyrics"

loch-lomond.text: Maxine Sullivan's swing version, recorded in August 1937 to Claude Thornhill's arrangement, was such a hit that it made her famous and led her to swing more folk songs.

the-water-is-wide.text: An old relative of the song, Waly, Waly, Gin Love Be Bonny, was in print by the 1720s: in Thomson's Orpheus Caledonius, usually dated 1725, and in the second volume of Allan Ramsay's Tea-Table Miscellany, published in Edinburgh before 1727.
the-water-is-wide.source: Francis James Child, The English and Scottish Popular Ballads, vol. 4 (1890), No. 204, p. 92

the-water-is-wide.text: Cecil Sharp heard it in Somerset five times, with tunes and words varying a lot, and printed a version in 1906 in Folk Songs from Somerset.
the-water-is-wide.source: Just Another Tune, "The Water Is Wide" (quoting Sharp's note in Folk Songs From Somerset, Third Series, 1906)

the-water-is-wide.text: Some of its verses also appear in the old ballad Jamie Douglas, which tells of Lady Douglas being put away by her husband in 1681.
the-water-is-wide.source: University of Toronto Libraries, Representative Poetry Online, "Waly, Waly", note

the-water-is-wide.text: Hymnals call the tune O Waly Waly. Its four lines of eight syllables fit many hymns, among them When I Survey the Wondrous Cross.

steal-away.text: In The Souls of Black Folk (1903), W. E. B. Du Bois picked ten master songs among the spirituals, and called the last of them, Steal Away, the song of songs.
steal-away.source: W. E. B. Du Bois, The Souls of Black Folk (1903), "The Sorrow Songs" (Standard Ebooks edition)

steal-away.text: In an 1880 printing, every verse and the chorus end on the same line, and each verse shares its third line too: only the opening pictures change, from thunder to bending trees, lightning and bursting tombstones.
steal-away.source: University of Virginia, Uncle Tom's Cabin & American Culture, "Steal Away" (text from J. B. T. Marsh, The Story of the Jubilee Singers With Their Songs, 1880)

steal-away.text: Gospel Pearls, a 1921 hymnal from the National Baptist Convention's publishing board, printed it as Steal Away to Jesus, in an arrangement by the Work Brothers.
steal-away.source: Hymnary.org, "Gospel Pearls" (1921), no. 155 "Steal Away to Jesus"

steal-away.text: Michael Tippett made it the first of the five spirituals in his oratorio A Child of Our Time.
steal-away.source: Opera Today, "Tippett: A Child of Our Time, BBC Prom 25" (2012)

down-by-the-old-mill-stream.text: The 1910 sheet music came with an extra setting of the chorus for men's voices, arranged by Charles Miller.
down-by-the-old-mill-stream.source: IMSLP, "Down by the Old Mill Stream (Taylor, Tell)", Misc. Notes

down-by-the-old-mill-stream.text: By 1948 the music historian Sigmund Spaeth noted that audiences were being taught to sing it with detailed comic gestures.
down-by-the-old-mill-stream.source: The Traditional Ballad Index, "Down by the Old Mill Stream", Notes (citing Sigmund Spaeth, A History of Popular Music in America, 1948, p. 372)

down-by-the-old-mill-stream.text: A later chart history ranks it the third most popular song in America in 1911, peaking at number three that July.
down-by-the-old-mill-stream.source: The Traditional Ballad Index (Robert B. Waltz and David G. Engle), "Down by the Old Mill Stream", Notes

keep-on-the-sunny-side.text: The Carter Family recorded it in Camden, New Jersey, in 1928, and it became their familiar theme song.
keep-on-the-sunny-side.source: Smithsonian Folkways, liner notes by Hal Bruno to The DeBusk-Weaver Family, "Meeting in the Air" (FTS 32431, 1979)

keep-on-the-sunny-side.text: It appeared in 1899 in Bright Melodies, a Philadelphia songbook by John R. Sweney and J. Howard Entwisle, who wrote its music. It has since been printed in at least 55 hymnals.
keep-on-the-sunny-side.source: Hymnary.org, "There's a dark and a troubled side of life" (text page)

keep-on-the-sunny-side.text: Ada Blenkhorn, who wrote the words, was born in Cobourg, Ontario, the 10th of 11 children, and began writing hymn lyrics at 34. Hymnary.org lists hundreds of her texts.
Johnny Cash wrote of visiting A.P. Carter's grave in Virginia: set into the marble monument was a gold record bearing this song's title.
keep-on-the-sunny-side.source: JohnnyCash.com, Johnny Cash's liner notes for the album Keep On the Sunny Side

let-me-call-you-sweetheart.text: It's a waltz, but in September 1925 a New Orleans band, the Halfway House Orchestra, recorded it as jazz, out of waltz time.
let-me-call-you-sweetheart.source: Library of Congress, National Recording Registry essay by David Sager, "Let Me Call You Sweetheart"

let-me-call-you-sweetheart.text: It was registered for copyright in April 1910, yet only three recordings of it came out in the 1910s. Then it vanished from records until 1924.
let-me-call-you-sweetheart.source: Library of Congress, National Recording Registry essay by David Sager, "Let Me Call You Sweetheart", The Columbia Quartette (The Peerless Quartet) (1911)

let-me-call-you-sweetheart.text: The 1911 record added to the National Recording Registry in 2015 was labeled the Columbia Quartette, but the singers were the Peerless Quartet, led by tenor Henry Burr.
let-me-call-you-sweetheart.source: Library of Congress, National Recording Registry essay by David Sager, "Let Me Call You Sweetheart"

let-me-call-you-sweetheart.text: In the mid-1920s two records helped make it a standard: a plain country version and a wistful close-harmony one by the Shannon Quartet. Heard on them, a 1910 song seemed a decade or two older than it was.
let-me-call-you-sweetheart.source: Library of Congress, National Recording Registry essay by David Sager, "Let Me Call You Sweetheart"

now-is-the-month-of-maying.text: In his 1597 music textbook, Morley said balletts, also called fa las, were songs for dancing as well as singing, and that the first set he had seen was by the Italian Gastoldi.
now-is-the-month-of-maying.source: Thomas Morley, A Plaine and Easie Introduction to Practicall Musicke (1597), excerpt "Thomas Morley on Kinds of Vocal Music", University of Mississippi course page

now-is-the-month-of-maying.text: Earlier English editors put English words to unchanged Italian pieces. For his 1595 balletts, Morley instead wrote new music loosely modeled on Italian ones.
now-is-the-month-of-maying.source: Megan Kaes Long, "Characteristic Tonality in the Balletti of Gastoldi, Morley, and Hassler", Journal of Music Theory (abstract), Oberlin College Digital Commons

now-is-the-month-of-maying.text: Morley's book of balletts came out in 1595 in two editions from the same London printer, Thomas Este: one in English and one with Italian words.
now-is-the-month-of-maying.source: IMSLP, "Balletts to Five Voyces, Book 1 (Morley, Thomas)"

sweet-adeline.text: Boston politician John F. Fitzgerald, President Kennedy's grandfather, got his nickname Honey Fitz from his love of singing songs like this one at rallies.
sweet-adeline.source: National Park Service, "John Fitzgerald: Mayor of a Bigger, Better, Busier Boston"

sweet-adeline.text: When Fitzgerald died in 1950, people gathered outside sang it as his coffin was carried to the cemetery.
sweet-adeline.source: National Park Service, "John Fitzgerald: Mayor of a Bigger, Better, Busier Boston"

wade-in-the-water.text: Fisk University's New Jubilee Songs, second edition (1904), prints it as "a favorite melody among Southern Baptists while a baptism is in progress." Though the book's preface says most of its songs were harmonized, this one is printed as a bare tune.
wade-in-the-water.source: Frederick J. Work, New Jubilee Songs as Sung by the Fisk Jubilee Singers, 2nd ed. (Fisk University, 1904), preface and pp. 8 and 9; Auburn Avenue Research Library, via the Digital Library of Georgia

wade-in-the-water.text: Harry T. Burleigh set it for voice and piano in 1925, as Wade in de Water. Near the end he lifts "Wade in de water" an octave, for a broader, louder climax.
wade-in-the-water.source: H. T. Burleigh, arr., "Wade in de water" (G. Ricordi, copyright 1925), pp. 37 to 41, University of Toronto copy; Catalog of Copyright Entries, 1925, part 3, p. 1041, entry 21432

wade-in-the-water.text: Alvin Ailey's dance Revelations, first performed in 1960, uses it in the section Take Me to the Water. His company calls Revelations the most widely seen modern dance work in the world.
wade-in-the-water.source: Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater, "Revelations by Alvin Ailey", AILEY Dance Repertory

wade-in-the-water.text: In 1994 NPR released a 26-part radio series on African American sacred music and titled it Wade in the Water.
wade-in-the-water.source: NPR, "Wade In The Water Ep. 6: Lined Hymn & Shaped-Note Tradition"

it-is-well.text: This hymn was first printed in 1876, as No. 76 in Gospel Hymns No. 2, the songbook Philip Bliss and Ira Sankey made for their revival meetings. These are Bliss's own four parts from that page.
it-is-well.source: Gospel Hymns No. 2 (1876), No. 76, read from the scan

it-is-well.text: In the chorus the tune holds "well" and "soul" while the other parts answer "it is well" underneath: Bliss wrote the echo into the parts himself.
it-is-well.source: Gospel Hymns No. 2 (1876), No. 76, read from the scan

hey-ho-nobody-home.text: This round was printed in 1609 in Pammelia, the earliest printed English book of rounds and catches, credited to Thomas Ravenscroft. There it is a round for five voices.
hey-ho-nobody-home.source: [Thomas Ravenscroft, compiler], Pammelia (London: William Barley, 1609), p. 41, No. 85, read from the facsimile (the 1971 Da Capo Press reprint, also on IMSLP); and William H. Husk, "Pammelia", in George Grove, ed., A Dictionary of Music and Musicians, vol. 2 (London: Macmillan, 1880), p. 643

hey-ho-nobody-home.text: The 1609 words end "fill the pot, Eadie": a call to fill the drinking pot. The ending many people know today, "yet will I be merry", came much later.
hey-ho-nobody-home.source: Thomas Ravenscroft, Pammelia (1609), No. 85, read from the facsimile (also on IMSLP)

daisy-bell.text: Harry Dacre's song was published in 1892, marked Tempo di Valse: a waltz. Its sheet music prints three verses under one tune.
daisy-bell.source: Daisy Bell, sheet music (T. B. Harms & Co., copyright 1892; this copy printed 1893 or later), read from the scan

daisy-bell.text: The chorus is marked "a little faster" than the verse, and it is the part almost everyone knows: "Daisy, Daisy, give me your answer, do".
daisy-bell.source: Daisy Bell, sheet music (T. B. Harms & Co., copyright 1892; this copy printed 1893 or later), read from the scan

ave-verum-corpus.text: Mozart wrote this short motet in 1791, the last year of his life. Its catalogue number is K. 618.
ave-verum-corpus.source: Mozart's Werke, Serie 3, No. 31 (Breitkopf & Härtel, 1880), read from the scan

ave-verum-corpus.text: Mozart marked it Adagio and sotto voce, "under the voice": slow, and soft all the way through. There is not one loud note in it.
ave-verum-corpus.source: Mozart's Werke, Serie 3, No. 31 (Breitkopf & Härtel, 1880), read from the scan

la-paloma.text: Sebastián Iradier called it a "canción americana", an American song, and it was in print in Madrid by 1859. Its words begin as a man leaves Havana.
la-paloma.source: Boletín bibliográfico español, vol. 2 (Madrid, 1861), p. 122, entry 917, read from the scan; La Paloma (Century Music Publishing, 1906), read from the scan

la-paloma.text: Under the tune the piano plays the habanera rhythm all the way through: a long note, a short one, then two even ones. Here the bass sings it.
la-paloma.source: La Paloma (Century Music Publishing, 1906), read from the scan

sakura-sakura.text: This song's earliest known printing is from 1888, by Tokyo's music school, in a collection of music for the koto, a long zither, with the tune written in Western notes.
sakura-sakura.source: Sōkyokushū (Ministry of Education, Tokyo, 1888), No. 2, read from the scan

sakura-sakura.text: The tune uses only five notes, the in scale of Japanese koto music, and ends on a note that sounds open rather than finished.
sakura-sakura.source: Sōkyokushū (Ministry of Education, Tokyo, 1888), No. 2, read from the scan

holy-holy-holy.text: In Hymns Ancient and Modern, the 1861 book that first printed this tune, it is Hymn 135, the hymn for Trinity Sunday.
holy-holy-holy.source: Hymns Ancient and Modern, with accompanying tunes (Novello, 1861), Hymn 135, read from the scan

holy-holy-holy.text: The book's index marks Nicaea as a new tune, written for it by John Bacchus Dykes, who harmonised it too: these are his own four parts.
holy-holy-holy.source: Hymns Ancient and Modern, with accompanying tunes (Novello, 1861), Hymn 135, read from the scan

with-cat-like-tread.text: The pirates sing about creeping in silence, but Sullivan marks their chorus Allegro marziale, like a march, and it gets louder as it goes: the joke is in the music.
with-cat-like-tread.source: The Pirates of Penzance, vocal score (Chappell), Act II No. 12, read from the scan

with-cat-like-tread.text: Two choruses sing at once here: the pirates creep along "with cat-like tread" while the police answer "Tarantara!", each chorus in two parts.
with-cat-like-tread.source: The Pirates of Penzance, vocal score (Chappell), Act II No. 12, read from the scan

haul-away-joe.text: This is the tune John Short, an old sailor from the harbour town of Watchet, sang to Cecil Sharp, who printed it in English Folk-Chanteys in 1914.
haul-away-joe.source: Cecil J. Sharp, English Folk-Chanteys (1914), No. XXVII and its note, read from the scan

haul-away-joe.text: Tozer, Bullen and Whall print this shanty in a major key; Sharp notes that John Short's tune is in the dorian mode, which gives it its darker sound.
haul-away-joe.source: Cecil J. Sharp, English Folk-Chanteys (1914), No. XXVII and its note, read from the scan

asleep-in-the-deep.text: H. W. Petrie's song of 1897 was sold as a "Song for Baritone or Bass Voice", which is why here the bass, not the soprano, sings the tune.
asleep-in-the-deep.source: "Asleep in the Deep" (New York: F. A. Mills), Lester S. Levy Sheet Music Collection, Johns Hopkins University, Box 145, Item 046, read from the scan

asleep-in-the-deep.text: The last line keeps its lowest notes for the end: it is sung twice, the second time sinking through "asleep in the deep" to a last "beware!" a whole octave below the first.
asleep-in-the-deep.source: "Asleep in the Deep" (New York: F. A. Mills), Lester S. Levy Sheet Music Collection, Johns Hopkins University, Box 145, Item 046, read from the scan

go-down-moses.text: The Fisk Jubilee Singers' book of 1872 gives Go Down, Moses twenty-four verses, from Israel in Egypt to the Red Sea and on to freedom.
go-down-moses.source: Theodore F. Seward, Jubilee Songs: As Sung by the Jubilee Singers of Fisk University (New York: Biglow & Main, 1872), pp. 22 to 23, read from the scan

go-down-moses.text: In that first printing only the answer, "Let my people go", is written in four-part harmony; every call is printed as the tune alone.
go-down-moses.source: Theodore F. Seward, Jubilee Songs: As Sung by the Jubilee Singers of Fisk University (New York: Biglow & Main, 1872), pp. 22 to 23, read from the scan

brahms-lullaby.text: Brahms wrote it as a gift for his friend Bertha Faber, on the birth of her second son.
brahms-lullaby.source: OMI facsimile of the autograph presentation copy (sent 15 July 1868 to Arthur and Bertha Faber for the birth of their second son, Hans); and Georg Predota, "Sing, sleep, honey", Interlude (2016)

brahms-lullaby.text: The Brahms-Institut records its first documented public performance in Vienna in December 1869, sung by Luise Dustmann with Clara Schumann at the piano.
brahms-lullaby.source: Brahms-Institut an der Musikhochschule Lübeck, Werkekatalog, Op. 49 (first documented performance, Vienna, 22 December 1869, Louise Dustmann, Clara Schumann); and Max Kalbeck, Johannes Brahms, vol. 2 (1908), p. 331 (Clara Schumann's Vienna concerts of December 1869 to January 1870, where Luise Dustmann sang Brahms songs from Op. 49)

joy-to-the-world.text: Lowell Mason's earliest known printing of this tune, which he called Antioch, is from 1836, "Arranged from Handel" and set to Watts's Psalm 98, with the tenor and bass already coming in behind on "And heav'n and nature sing".
joy-to-the-world.source: Lowell Mason, Occasional Psalm and Hymn Tunes, No. 3 (Boston, copyright 1836), No. 73, "Antioch", p. 70, read from the scan

joy-to-the-world.text: In The National Psalmist of 1848, Mason added a footnote that the tune had been "very popular for Choir and Singing School practice" and should perhaps be kept mainly to that, since "it cannot be appropriate to many Psalms, Hymns, or to the ordinary circumstances of Public Worship".
joy-to-the-world.source: Lowell Mason and George James Webb, The National Psalmist (Boston, 1848), p. 132, footnote, read from the scan; quoted in Chris Fenner, "Joy to the world", Hymnology Archive (2018, rev. 2022)

hark-the-herald.text: Mendelssohn wrote this tune in 1840 for a festival song in Leipzig, honouring Gutenberg and what was taken to be 400 years of printing. It was not written for Christmas at all.
hark-the-herald.source: James T. Lightwood, Hymn-Tunes and Their Story (London, [1906]), pp. 340 to 341, and The Praise Trust, "Hark! The herald angels sing"

hark-the-herald.text: An organist at Waltham Abbey, William Hayman Cummings, fitted Mendelssohn's music to Charles Wesley's words in the 1850s, and the pairing stuck.
hark-the-herald.source: James T. Lightwood, Hymn-Tunes and Their Story (London, [1906]), pp. 340 to 341, and The Praise Trust, "Hark! The herald angels sing"

jingle-bells.text: Oliver Ditson of Boston published James Lord Pierpont's song in 1857 as The One Horse Open Sleigh. It is about a sleigh ride, with no word of Christmas; it became a Christmas song only later.
jingle-bells.source: Joel Brown, "Unearthing the Truth about 'Jingle Bells'", Bostonia, Boston University (9 December 2016), and Christopher Klein, "8 Things You May Not Know About 'Jingle Bells'", History.com

jingle-bells.text: On 16 December 1965 two astronauts on Gemini 6 played it in orbit, on a tiny harmonica and a handful of small bells: the first musical instruments played in space, NASA says. Both now belong to the Smithsonian.
jingle-bells.source: National Air and Space Museum, "Tom Stafford's Jingle Bells and Wally Schirra's Harmonica" (16 December 2014), and John Uri, "55 Years Ago: The Spirit of 76, The First Rendezvous in Space", NASA (8 December 2020)

god-rest-ye.text: It is carol number 1, the first in the book, in Bramley and Stainer's Christmas Carols New and Old, whose first series came out in 1867.
god-rest-ye.source: H. R. Bramley and John Stainer, Christmas Carols New and Old, first series (Novello, 1867; an 1870s printing), No. 1 and its index, read from the scan

god-rest-ye.text: That book gives both its words and its tune as simply traditional: nobody knows who first sang it.
god-rest-ye.source: H. R. Bramley and John Stainer, Christmas Carols New and Old, first series (Novello, 1867; an 1870s printing), No. 1 and its index, read from the scan

deck-the-halls.text: The tune is Welsh: Nos Galan, which means New Year's Eve. It was in print by 1781, in John Parry's British Harmony, and the harpist Edward Jones printed it in 1784.
deck-the-halls.source: John Parry, British Harmony (Ruabon and London, 1781), p. 12, No. 7, and Edward Jones, Musical and Poetical Relicks of the Welsh Bards (London, 1784), p. 64, read from the scans

deck-the-halls.text: The English words, "Deck the hall with boughs of holly", are by the Scottish musician Thomas Oliphant, written for a book of Welsh melodies printed in London in 1862.
deck-the-halls.source: John Thomas, Welsh Melodies, vol. 2 (London, 1862), No. 15, p. 139, "The English Poetry by T. Oliphant Esq.", facsimile hosted by Handy Finch; John Hullah, The Song Book (1866), p. 325; Dictionary of National Biography, vol. 42 (1895), "Oliphant, Thomas" (Scottish, born at Condie, Perthshire)

away-in-a-manger.text: Early books credited the words to Martin Luther, and James R. Murray's songbook of 1887 said Luther wrote them for his children. Historians now reject that: the words are anonymous, and in print in America by 1882.
away-in-a-manger.source: Richard S. Hill, "Not So Far Away in a Manger", Notes (Music Library Association, December 1945), and Hymnology Archive, "Away in a manger" (2018, revised 2023)

away-in-a-manger.text: William J. Kirkpatrick's tune, Cradle Song, has its earliest known printing in 1895, in Around the World with Christmas, a Christmas exercise for Sunday schools. It is the usual tune in Britain; in the United States, James R. Murray's tune, Mueller, is more common.
away-in-a-manger.source: Canterbury Dictionary of Hymnology, "Away in a manger" (Canterbury Press, 2013), and Richard S. Hill, "Not So Far Away in a Manger", Notes (December 1945)

abide-with-me.text: Henry Francis Lyte wrote it in 1847, in failing health, shortly before he left England for the warmer south. He died at Nice that November.
abide-with-me.source: Henry Francis Lyte, Remains (1850), memoir pp. l to lvi and the hymn signed "Berry Head, September, 1847"; and Chris Fenner, Abide with me, Hymnology Archive; also Canterbury Dictionary of Hymnology, "Henry Francis Lyte"

abide-with-me.text: It has been sung before the FA Cup Final in England since 1927, the year it was introduced there.
abide-with-me.source: Cardiff City FC, "90 years: a final of firsts" (2017); and Barry Richards, Bournemouth University ("introduced at the 1927 final"); also Public Domain Review, "Abide With Me (1914)"

shall-we-gather.text: Its earliest known printing, in 1865, called it Beautiful River. The tune was later named Hanson Place, after the Brooklyn Baptist church where Robert Lowry was pastor when he wrote it.
shall-we-gather.source: Hymnary.org, "Shall We Gather at the River?", text and tune notes; Chris Fenner, "Shall we gather at the river", Hymnology Archive (2018, revised 2025); Happy Voices (New York: American Tract Society, 1865), No. 220

shall-we-gather.text: It was one of the film director John Ford's favourite hymns, and he used it in many of his westerns, Stagecoach and The Searchers among them.
shall-we-gather.source: BBC Music Magazine, "Shall We Gather at the River lyrics", classical-music.com (2022); Tim Dirks, "Stagecoach (1939)", Filmsite; Craig Lysy, reviews of the Stagecoach and The Searchers scores, Movie Music UK (2024, 2017)

jerusalem.text: Parry wrote the music on 10 March 1916, at the request of the poet Robert Bridges, for the Fight for Right movement. It was first sung at the movement's meeting in London's Queen's Hall on 28 March.
jerusalem.source: Jeremy Dibble, "Jerusalem: A Hymn to Women's Suffrage", Culture Matters (2016); "Jerusalem the Golden", Standpoint (22 April 2013, unsigned), quoting Parry's diary for 10 March 1916; Jason Whittaker, Prospect (26 December 2019)

jerusalem.text: Campaigners for women's votes took it up in 1918, and Parry wrote to their leader, Millicent Fawcett, that he wished it might become the Women Voters' hymn.
jerusalem.source: Jeremy Dibble, "Jerusalem: A Hymn to Women's Suffrage", Culture Matters (2016); Jason Whittaker, Prospect (2019); "Jerusalem the Golden", Standpoint (22 April 2013, unsigned)

o-holy-night.text: By the usual account, Placide Cappeau wrote the French words in December 1847, in a stagecoach between Mâcon and Dijon. Adolphe Adam set them within days, and they were first sung at Midnight Mass in Roquemaure that Christmas.
o-holy-night.source: Denis Havard de la Montagne, "Minuit Chrétiens, une partition d'Adolphe Adam", Musica et Memoria, and "Origine gardoise du Minuit Chrétiens", Nemausensis (Nîmes, 2011)

o-holy-night.text: John Sullivan Dwight, the Boston music critic and former Unitarian minister who wrote the English words in 1855, hated slavery. His line "Chains shall he break, for the slave is our brother" grows from Cappeau's French.
o-holy-night.source: George Willis Cooke, John Sullivan Dwight, Brook-Farmer, Editor, and Critic of Music (Boston, 1898), ch. VII, and Delaney Coyne, "The abolitionist history of 'O Holy Night'", America (26 November 2023)

come-thou-fount.text: Robert Robinson wrote the words in his early twenties. His own list of his writings dates the hymn to 1758, and its earliest surviving printing is in a London hymnbook of 1759.
come-thou-fount.source: Hymnology Archive, "Come, thou fount of every blessing"; and Canterbury Dictionary of Hymnology, "Come, thou fount of every blessing"; also Hymnary.org (born 27 September 1735)

come-thou-fount.text: The tune's earliest known printing is in John Wyeth's Repository of Sacred Music, Part Second, in 1813. It is named after the preacher Asahel Nettleton, and some books credit him with it, but who wrote it is not known.
come-thou-fount.source: Hymnology Archive, "Come, thou fount of every blessing"; and Psalter Hymnal Handbook at Hymnary.org, NETTLETON

the-lord-bless-you.text: Peter Lutkin was the first dean of Northwestern University's School of Music, which by the university's own history he led from 1895 until 1928.
the-lord-bless-you.source: Northwestern University Bienen School of Music, "History"; Chris Fenner, "The Lord bless you and keep you", Hymnology Archive (2018)

the-lord-bless-you.text: The Methodist Hymnal of 1905 prints this blessing as No. 748, with a short two-bar Amen in place of Lutkin's sevenfold one.
the-lord-bless-you.source: The Methodist Hymnal (New York: Eaton & Mains, 1905), No. 748, p. 532, read from the scan

lift-every-voice.text: James Weldon Johnson wrote the poem for a celebration of Abraham Lincoln's birthday in Jacksonville, Florida, in 1900, where a choir of 500 schoolchildren first sang it.
lift-every-voice.source: NAACP, "Lift Every Voice and Sing", History Explained; Chris Fenner, "Lift every voice and sing", Hymnology Archive (2019), quoting Johnson's own account; Cait Miller, Library of Congress In the Muse blog (8 February 2022)

lift-every-voice.text: By 1920 the NAACP was calling it the "Negro national anthem".
lift-every-voice.source: Cait Miller, "Lift Every Voice and Sing", Library of Congress In the Muse blog (2022); Burton W. Peretti, "Lift Ev'ry Voice and Sing", National Recording Registry essay, Library of Congress

nearer-my-god.text: Sarah Flower Adams wrote it for Hymns and Anthems, the hymn book of William Johnson Fox's chapel in London, in print by 1841. It retells Jacob's dream in Genesis 28, of a ladder between earth and heaven.
nearer-my-god.source: Canterbury Dictionary of Hymnology, "Nearer, my God, to thee" (Canterbury Press); Hymnary.org, "Nearer, My God, to Thee", text notes

nearer-my-god.text: Some Titanic survivors said the ship's band played it as she sank; others denied it, so no one knows for sure.
nearer-my-god.source: Archibald Gracie, The Truth about the Titanic (New York: Mitchell Kennerley, 1913), ch. 1; NPR Morning Edition, "Remembering The Titanic's Intrepid Bandleader" (13 April 2012)

greensleeves.text: Shakespeare names it twice in The Merry Wives of Windsor, where Falstaff cries, "Let the sky rain potatoes, let it thunder to the tune of Greensleeves."
greensleeves.source: Folger Shakespeare, The Merry Wives of Windsor 5.5 (FTLN 2675-2676); and The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT), Merry Wives 2.1 and 5.5

greensleeves.text: People were singing Christmas-season words to this tune by the 1600s. The best known today, "What Child Is This?", are by William Chatterton Dix, in print by 1871.
greensleeves.source: The Oxford Book of Carols (1928), No. 28, "The Old Year Now Away Is Fled", from New Christmas Carols (1642) "to the tune of Greensleeves"; and Douglas D. Anderson, Hymns and Carols of Christmas, "What Child Is This" (citing Keyte and Parrott, New Oxford Book of Carols)

leave-her-johnny.text: Cecil Sharp wrote that sailors usually sang it as the ship was getting into port, the shantyman using it to say what the crew thought of the ship they were about to leave.
leave-her-johnny.source: Cecil J. Sharp, English Folk-Chanteys (1914), note to No. 2, Internet Archive

leave-her-johnny.text: Cecil Sharp put it among the capstan shanties, for steady work like marching round the capstan or working the pumps, not among the pulling ones. He called this version the usual form of the tune.
leave-her-johnny.source: Cecil J. Sharp, English Folk-Chanteys (1914), contents, introduction and note to No. 2, Internet Archive

drunken-sailor.text: The old sea captain W. B. Whall wrote that the whole crew sang it together at a quick march, as they walked away with the rope. When crews got smaller and could no longer walk away with anything, the song dropped out of use.
drunken-sailor.source: W. B. Whall, Ships, Sea Songs and Shanties (3rd ed., 1913), p. 107, Internet Archive

drunken-sailor.text: Richard Terry, who printed this tune in 1921, named it as one of the shanties in the old modes, rather than in a modern major or minor key.
drunken-sailor.source: R. R. Terry, The Shanty Book, Part I (1921), introduction, Internet Archive

caro-mio-ben.text: Alessandro Parisotti's popular anthologies credited it to Giuseppe Giordani, and many books still do. Later research points to Tommaso Giordani: an early London print, of about 1785, says the singer Pacchierotti sang it at a concert there.
caro-mio-ben.source: IMSLP, Caro mio ben (Giordani, Tommaso), the London print by John Preston (ca. 1785); and Katie Buzard, Illinois Public Media, Clef Notes (2024); also Art Song Central, Giordani: Caro mio ben

caro-mio-ben.text: It is often the first art song a voice teacher gives a new student: slow, gentle, and in a comfortable range.
caro-mio-ben.source: Todd Edward Ranney, Vocal Preparation for the High School Male, DMA document, Ohio State University (2009); and Katie Buzard, Illinois Public Media (2024)

shorty-george-blues.text: Hociel Thomas, who wrote the words with her father George W. Thomas, became a blues singer and pianist herself, and made records in the mid-1920s.
shorty-george-blues.source: Shorty George Blues (Chicago: Geo. W. Thomas Music Co., 1924), title page; James Head, "Thomas, Hociel", Handbook of Texas Online, Texas State Historical Association (2006, revised 2017); Bill Edwards, "George Washington Thomas", RagPiano.com

shorty-george-blues.text: George W. Thomas ran his own music publishing company in Chicago, and printed this song himself in 1924.
shorty-george-blues.source: Shorty George Blues (Chicago: Geo. W. Thomas Music Co., copyright 1924 by Geo. W. Thomas); Bill Edwards, "George Washington Thomas", RagPiano.com; "George and Hersal Thomas", San Diego Ragtime essay

deep-river.text: In Burleigh's setting the altos sing the tune. The sopranos wait eight bars, then float the refrain above the altos' second time through, mostly on long notes. In the verse both sing the tune together, until the sopranos climb alone on "That promised land".
deep-river.source: H. T. Burleigh, Deep River, for mixed voices (New York: G. Schirmer, 1914), pp. 1 to 3, read from the scan

deep-river.text: Deep River was in print by 1875, in the second edition of J. B. T. Marsh's The Story of the Jubilee Singers; with Their Songs, a book about Fisk University's touring singers.
deep-river.source: J. B. T. Marsh, The Story of the Jubilee Singers; with Their Songs, second edition (London: Hodder and Stoughton, 1875), No. 77, pp. 196 to 197, Universitätsbibliothek Gießen, Gb 4660; and University of Pittsburgh, Voices Across Time, "Deep River"

white-coral-bells.text: The earliest known printing of this round is "May Bells", in Hollis Dann's Fourth Year Music, a school music reader of 1916. It is printed for two voices, the second coming in at the fifth bar.
white-coral-bells.source: Hollis Dann Music Course, Fourth Year Music (American Book Company, 1916), p. 115, read from the scan

white-coral-bells.text: Dann's book names no author for it, nor for any of its other rounds. The Traditional Ballad Index files it as a camp song found in the US, and notes that it may be sung as a round.
white-coral-bells.source: Hollis Dann Music Course, Fourth Year Music (American Book Company, 1916), its rounds on pp. 32, 47, 92, 101, 106, 109, 115 and 125, read from the scan; and The Traditional Ballad Index, "White Coral Bells"

londons-burning.text: John Goss printed this round in 1927 in the Daily Express Community Song Book, made for the newspaper's community singing movement. He numbers its four lines for the four voices to come in, one after another.
londons-burning.source: "Daily Express" Community Song Book, ed. John Goss (London, 1927), p. 195, read from the scan

londons-burning.text: A version called "Scotland's Burning" was printed in America in 1816, as a canon in four numbered lines, in David Vinton's The Masonick Minstrel. It sings "Look out" where London's Burning has "Fetch the engines".
londons-burning.source: David Vinton, The Masonick Minstrel (Dedham, Massachusetts, 1816), p. 21, read from the scan

three-blind-mice.text: In 1886 a reader of the journal Notes and Queries called Three Blind Mice "the school round", and wrote that in all the copies of the round he had met the words ran "They all ran after the farmer's wife".
three-blind-mice.source: Notes and Queries, 7th series, vol. 2 (25 December 1886), p. 507, read from the scan

three-blind-mice.text: Our version is read from Home Songs, a Boston collection of 1906 of favourite songs, hymns and rounds "for the fireside", which prints it as a round in four parts.
three-blind-mice.source: Home Songs (Oliver Ditson Company, Boston, 1906), p. 95, read from the scan

oh-how-lovely.text: The tune is a German round, "O wie wohl ist mir am Abend", in print by 1842 with no composer named. Later books credit a Schulz but disagree on which one, so who made it is not certain.
oh-how-lovely.source: Theodor Fliedner, ed., Lieder-Buch für Kleinkinder-Schulen (Kaiserswerth, 1842), p. 29, No. 54, read from the scan; H. Liebhart, Liederlust und Psalter (Cincinnati, 1882), p. 193, signed "Schulz.", read from the scan; Lieder-Projekt (Carus-Verlag and SWR2), "O wie wohl ist mir am Abend"; Der Große Brockhaus, vol. 14 (Leipzig, copyright 1933), p. 27, read from the scan

oh-how-lovely.text: A Toronto school songbook of 1869 printed an earlier English version, "Oh, How Lovely!", a round for three voices, with "When to rest the bells are ringing", closer to the German, where later books have "When the bells are sweetly ringing".
oh-how-lovely.source: H. F. Sefton, Three-Part Songs (Toronto, 1869), p. 41, read from the scan

ezekiel-saw-the-wheel.text: Its songbook marks the refrain for everyone, "Tutti", and the first line of each verse for one voice, "Solo quasi extempore sed meme ritmo": as if made up on the spot, but in the same rhythm. The second line is marked "Solo capriccioso".
ezekiel-saw-the-wheel.source: R. Nathaniel Dett, ed., Religious Folk-Songs of the Negro as Sung at Hampton Institute (Hampton, Va., 1927), pp. 60 and 61, read from the scan

ezekiel-saw-the-wheel.text: The same book files it among its "Hymns on Biblical Themes", marked "Poco allegro ritmo marcato": fairly lively, with a firm, marked rhythm.
ezekiel-saw-the-wheel.source: R. Nathaniel Dett, ed., Religious Folk-Songs of the Negro as Sung at Hampton Institute (1927), p. 60, read from the scan

every-time-i-feel-the-spirit.text: Robert R. Moton, who led the plantation songs at Hampton for nearly twenty years, wrote in 1909 that once students had caught the air, the best results usually came from letting them sing "as seems to them most easy and natural".
every-time-i-feel-the-spirit.source: Religious Folk Songs of the Negro, New Edition (Hampton, Va., 1909), "Note to New Edition", p. vi; reprinted in Dett's 1927 edition

every-time-i-feel-the-spirit.text: The songbook's editor, R. Nathaniel Dett, wrote that its tunes and harmonies were set down as the students sang them, in a tradition of singing these songs going back to 1868.
every-time-i-feel-the-spirit.source: R. Nathaniel Dett, ed., Religious Folk-Songs of the Negro as Sung at Hampton Institute (1927), introduction, section IX, p. xviii

were-you-there.text: The same songbook also prints a related spiritual, "Did You Hear How Dey Crucified My Lord?", and notes that "Were You There When They Crucified My Lord" seemed "to be universally more popular".
were-you-there.source: R. Nathaniel Dett, ed., Religious Folk-Songs of the Negro as Sung at Hampton Institute (1927), p. 104, read from the scan

were-you-there.text: Dett also wrote out his own version of it, trying, he said, "to transcribe the effect of the thousand voices of the school", in parts "so very simple and natural that no group of singers should be daunted by them".
were-you-there.source: R. Nathaniel Dett, ed., Religious Folk-Songs of the Negro as Sung at Hampton Institute (1927), p. 106, footnote, read from the scan

didnt-my-lord-deliver-daniel.text: For the Fisk Jubilee Singers' book of 1872, George L. White took the words down from the singers, and Theodore F. Seward wrote the music down; every melody was tested on the piano, and no line or phrase went in without the singers' full endorsement.
didnt-my-lord-deliver-daniel.source: Theodore F. Seward, Jubilee Songs (Biglow & Main, New York, 1872), introduction, read from the scan

didnt-my-lord-deliver-daniel.text: Seward noted that more than half the melodies in the Fisk singers' 1872 book use the same scale as Scottish music, the one that leaves out the fourth and seventh notes. Didn't My Lord Deliver Daniel is one of them: its tune uses only five notes.
didnt-my-lord-deliver-daniel.source: Theodore F. Seward, Jubilee Songs (1872), preface, p. 3, read from the scan; the song's notes, pp. 16 and 17

balm-in-gilead.text: This one is headed "Transcribed from the singing of the Hampton Institute students": the four parts were written down as the students sang them, and filed among the "Hymns of Consolation".
balm-in-gilead.source: R. Nathaniel Dett, ed., Religious Folk-Songs of the Negro as Sung at Hampton Institute (1927), p. 88, read from the scan

balm-in-gilead.text: Hampton's songbook was first published in 1874, when its student singers were giving concerts in the North to raise the walls of Virginia Hall.
balm-in-gilead.source: R. Nathaniel Dett, ed., Religious Folk-Songs of the Negro as Sung at Hampton Institute (1927), reprinting the preface to the edition of 1891, p. vii

bully-in-the-alley.text: Cecil Sharp took this chantey down from John Short of Watchet, and wrote that he had no other version of it and knew of no printed one.
bully-in-the-alley.source: Cecil J. Sharp, English Folk-Chanteys (London and Taunton, 1914), note to No. 35, p. 71, read from the scan

bully-in-the-alley.text: It is a pulling chantey: Sharp marks with arrow-heads the notes the crew pulled on, here two in each chorus, on "Way" and on the "bully" right after it.
bully-in-the-alley.source: Cecil J. Sharp, English Folk-Chanteys (1914), p. 32 (the note on arrow-heads) and pp. 40 and 41, read from the scan

haul-on-the-bowline.text: Sharp writes that the chanteyman often began by singing the refrain on his own, to announce the chantey he had chosen and remind the crew of the tune. This one starts that way.
haul-on-the-bowline.source: Cecil J. Sharp, English Folk-Chanteys (1914), introduction, p. xiii, and No. 37, pp. 42 and 43, read from the scan

haul-on-the-bowline.text: Sharp's singer had spent more than fifty years in sailing ships, and for most of them was a recognised chanteyman: the solo singer who led the chanteys.
haul-on-the-bowline.source: Cecil J. Sharp, English Folk-Chanteys (1914), introduction, p. xi, read from the scan

spanish-ladies.text: Sharp's singer, Captain Lewis of Minehead, sang it as a song, not as a chanty; round the capstan, Sharp notes, it went much faster, and he set his harmony for the slower pace.
spanish-ladies.source: Cecil J. Sharp, Folk Songs from Somerset, Fifth Series (1909), note to No. 124, pp. 89 and 90, read from the scan

spanish-ladies.text: Sharp prints the tune in its old minor form, and notes that sailors of his day sang a modernized major version, which he found "far less beautiful".
spanish-ladies.source: Cecil J. Sharp, Folk Songs from Somerset, Fifth Series (1909), note to No. 124, p. 90, read from the scan

blow-boys-blow.text: Richard Terry notes that spotless decks, and masts and yards that "shone like silver", were the marks of a Yankee packet ship, kept that way by a terrible discipline.
blow-boys-blow.source: R. R. Terry, The Shanty Book, Part I (London, 1921), note to No. 15, p. xv, read from the scan

blow-boys-blow.text: Terry prints it as a halliard shanty, for hoisting the sails: the shantyman sings each line alone and the crew answers "Blow, boys blow".
blow-boys-blow.source: R. R. Terry, The Shanty Book, Part I (1921), No. 15, pp. 32 and 33, read from the scan

maoz-tzur.text: The first letters of its stanzas spell the poet's name, Mordecai. He probably lived in the thirteenth century. The hymn was first sung at home, after lighting the Hanukkah lights, and later in the synagogue too.
maoz-tzur.source: The Jewish Encyclopedia, vol. 8 (1904), "Ma'oz Zur", by Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen

maoz-tzur.text: Eduard Birnbaum identified its tune as an adaptation of an old German folk song, "So weiss ich eins, dass mich erfreut", already widespread among German Jews by about 1450. Martin Luther set the same folk melody to one of his first chorales.

oy-chanukah.text: Susman Kisselgof printed it in his Yiddish songbook "for the Jewish school and family", first published in St Petersburg in 1911 and 1912, marking the tune "Chsidisch": a Hasidic melody.
oy-chanukah.source: Z. Kisselgof, Lider-zamelbukh far der yidisher shul un familye (4th ed., Berlin), No. 24, p. 32, read from the scan; first-edition preface dated St Petersburg, 1 June 1911

oy-chanukah.text: Mordkhe Rivesman's Yiddish words paint the holiday at home: dreidels every night, sizzling-hot latkes, then lighting the thin little candles and saying "Al hanisim", for the miracles.
oy-chanukah.source: Z. Kisselgof, Lider-zamelbukh, No. 24, words p. 13, read from the scan

ein-keloheinu.text: The Union Hymnal of 1897, the hymnal of the Central Conference of American Rabbis, prints it in four parts among its "Hebrew Hymns and Responses", with all five verses.
ein-keloheinu.source: The Union Hymnal (Central Conference of American Rabbis, 1897), No. 17, pp. 140 and 141, read from the scan

ein-keloheinu.text: The hymnal's 1932 edition credits it to Julius Freudenthal. The 1897 edition's index gives the music's source only as "German".
ein-keloheinu.source: The Union Hymnal (1932), No. 292, and (1897), index p. 218, read from the scans

adir-hu.text: The earliest known printing of its tune, in an early form, is in a Haggadah in Hebrew, Latin and German that J. S. Rittangel, a professor at Königsberg, published in 1644.
adir-hu.source: The Jewish Encyclopedia, vol. 1 (1901), "Addir Hu", by Francis L. Cohen, and A. Z. Idelsohn, Jewish Music in its Historical Development (1929), p. 174

adir-hu.text: A Judeo-German version, "Allmächtiger Gott, nun bau dein' Tempel schiere" (Almighty Hashem, now build Your Temple soon), was once widely sung, and Gottfried Selig printed it with the tune at Leipzig in 1769.
adir-hu.source: A. Z. Idelsohn, Jewish Music in its Historical Development (1929), pp. 174 and 504, and The Jewish Encyclopedia, vol. 1 (1901), "Addir Hu"

eliyahu-hanavi.text: Abraham Zvi Idelsohn printed this tune in 1929 in his history of Jewish music, among the "Tunes of the Eastern Ashkenazic folk-song".
eliyahu-hanavi.source: A. Z. Idelsohn, Jewish Music in its Historical Development (New York: Henry Holt, copyright 1929; read from the scan of the 1944 Tudor printing), p. 401, Table XXXII, No. 1

eliyahu-hanavi.text: Its words call on the prophet Elijah by three names: Elijah the prophet, Elijah the Tishbite, Elijah of Gilead.
eliyahu-hanavi.source: A. Z. Idelsohn, Jewish Music (1929), p. 401, the words printed under the tune

echad-mi-yodea.text: It counts from one to thirteen, and each stanza repeats every number back down to one: one is Hashem, in heaven and on earth.
echad-mi-yodea.source: The Union Haggadah (Central Conference of American Rabbis, 1923), pp. 86 to 92, read from the scan

echad-mi-yodea.text: The Union Haggadah of 1923 changes two of the numbers, in its Hebrew as well as its English: eight becomes the eight days of Hanukkah, and nine the nine festivals.
echad-mi-yodea.source: The Union Haggadah (1923), pp. 87 to 89, read from the scan

ki-lo-naeh.text: The Union Haggadah prints it as a solo verse and a chorus: one singer leads each verse, and everyone answers "Lecha ulecha", yours and yours.
ki-lo-naeh.source: The Union Haggadah (Central Conference of American Rabbis, 1923), pp. 84 and 85, read from the scan

ki-lo-naeh.text: It was already in the book's first edition of 1908, with the same tune in the same key, though with only its first verse.
ki-lo-naeh.source: The Union Haggadah (Central Conference of American Rabbis, 1908), pp. 54 and 55, read from the scan

lecha-dodi.text: Solomon ha-Levi Alkabetz wrote it about the middle of the sixteenth century to welcome the Sabbath, and signed eight of its nine verses with his name, their first letters spelling it out.
lecha-dodi.source: The Jewish Encyclopedia, vol. 7 (Funk and Wagnalls, 1904), p. 675, "Lekah Dodi", read from the archive.org text

lecha-dodi.text: The Jewish Encyclopedia says this tune was kept for the weeks of the Omer, between Passover and Shavuot, and that some heard "Lilliburlero" or Mozart's Figaro in its phrases, while it heard German folk song of the late seventeenth century.
lecha-dodi.source: The Jewish Encyclopedia, vol. 7 (Funk and Wagnalls, 1904), p. 675, "Lekah Dodi", read from the archive.org text

tzur-mishelo.text: It is one of the zemirot, the Hebrew songs sung at home around the table, most of all before or after the grace after the Sabbath's main meals.
tzur-mishelo.source: The Jewish Encyclopedia, vol. 12 (Funk and Wagnalls, 1906), p. 656, "Zemirot", read from the archive.org text

tzur-mishelo.text: The Jewish Encyclopedia names this German melody as the most frequent air for the table songs, sung with this song or with another, "Yom Zeh le-Yisrael".
tzur-mishelo.source: The Jewish Encyclopedia, vol. 12 (Funk and Wagnalls, 1906), p. 659, "Zemirot", read from the archive.org text

adon-olam.text: In Sephardic and British synagogues the whole congregation sings it at the close of the Sabbath and festival morning services, and it is chanted almost everywhere on the eve of Yom Kippur.
adon-olam.source: The Jewish Encyclopedia, vol. 1 (Funk and Wagnalls, 1901), p. 205, "Adon 'Olam", read from the archive.org text

adon-olam.text: Its closing lines, "Into His hand I commit my spirit when I fall asleep and when I awake", led the scholar Seligman Baer to think it was first meant to be said before going to sleep.
adon-olam.source: The Jewish Encyclopedia, vol. 1 (Funk and Wagnalls, 1901), p. 206, "Adon 'Olam", citing Baer's prayer-book commentary (Rödelheim, 1868), read from the archive.org text

shoshanat-yaakov.text: It is sung on Purim once the Book of Esther has been read: Baer's book has the scroll rolled up, the blessing sung after it, and then this song.
shoshanat-yaakov.source: Abraham Baer, Baal T'fillah (Frankfurt am Main: J. Kauffmann, 3rd edition), p. 59, Nos. 196 and 197, read from the scan

shoshanat-yaakov.text: On the same page Baer prints four verses of Esther that everyone sings aloud during the reading before the reader repeats them, starting with "Ish yehudi haya b'Shushan habira", there was a Jew in Shushan the capital.
shoshanat-yaakov.source: Abraham Baer, Baal T'fillah (Frankfurt am Main: J. Kauffmann, 3rd edition), p. 59, Nos. 192 to 195, "Chor, dann Solo", read from the scan

comin-thro-the-rye.text: The Scots Musical Museum prints the song twice: Burns's own words, "O Jenny's a' weet, poor body", to one tune, then on the next page a "2d Sett" with the tune sung today.
comin-thro-the-rye.source: The Scots Musical Museum, vol. 5 (Edinburgh: James Johnson; dated 1796 by the National Library of Scotland), pp. 430 and 431, Nos. 417 and 418, read from the scan; G. F. Graham, The Songs of Scotland, vol. II, p. 11, quoting Stenhouse ("This song was written by Burns")

comin-thro-the-rye.text: William Stenhouse wrote that the music-seller John Watlen "altered the first strain of the former tune a little, and published it with the new words. His edition had a considerable run."
comin-thro-the-rye.source: G. F. Graham, The Songs of Scotland, vol. II (Edinburgh: Wood and Co.), p. 11, quoting Stenhouse's notes on the Museum, read from the scan

red-red-rose.text: By the time of G. F. Graham's Songs of Scotland, the song was "now invariably sung to a modern version of 'Low down in the broom'", the tune we sing.
red-red-rose.source: G. F. Graham, The Songs of Scotland, vol. II (Edinburgh: Wood and Co.), p. 29, read from the scan

red-red-rose.text: Johnson's Scots Musical Museum set Burns's words to two other airs: a strathspey, "Major Graham", and an "Old Set" that G. F. Graham calls "Queen Mary's Lament".
red-red-rose.source: The Scots Musical Museum, vol. 5 (Edinburgh: James Johnson; dated 1796 by the National Library of Scotland), p. 415, Nos. 402 and 403, read from the scan; G. F. Graham, The Songs of Scotland, vol. II, p. 29

annie-laurie.text: Lady John Scott told the editor Alfred Moffat that the tune was her own, and that she altered the second verse and wrote all of the third.
annie-laurie.source: Alfred Moffat, The Minstrelsy of Scotland (London: Augener, 2nd edition), p. 109, footnote, read from the scan

annie-laurie.text: The older song is "said to" be by Mr Douglas of Fingland, for Anne, a daughter of Sir Robert Laurie of Maxwelton. But "the Lady afterwards married Mr Ferguson of Craigdarroch".
annie-laurie.source: C. K. Sharpe, A Ballad Book (1880 reprint of the 1823 edition), pp. 107 and 108, note, read from the scan

will-ye-no-come-back-again.text: Lady Nairne kept her authorship secret, even writing as "Mrs. Bogan, of Bogan". Only after she died did her sister agree, on January 16, 1846, to "letting it be known that she wrote them".
will-ye-no-come-back-again.source: Charles Rogers, Life and Songs of the Baroness Nairne (1869), memoir pp. xxxvi to xxxvii and lxxvii to lxxviii, read from the scan

will-ye-no-come-back-again.text: At Gask, where Lady Nairne grew up, a small table reads "Charles, Prince of Wales, breakfasted at this table in the low Drawing Room at Gask, September 11th, 1745." In 1900 his bonnet, brogues, spurs and a lock of his hair could still be seen there.
will-ye-no-come-back-again.source: George Henderson, Lady Nairne and Her Songs (1900), pp. 19 to 22, read from the scan

ye-banks-and-braes.text: The Scots Musical Museum's index credits the music to "Mr James Millar Writer in Edinr.": in Scotland, a writer was a lawyer.
ye-banks-and-braes.source: The Scots Musical Museum, vol. 4 (Edinburgh: James Johnson, 1792), index p. VI, No. 374, read from the scan

ye-banks-and-braes.text: Burns wrote that the organist Stephen Clarke, "partly by way of joke", told James Miller "to keep to the black keys of the harpsichord, and preserve some kind of rhythm, and he would infallibly compose a Scots air". In a few days Miller produced "the rudiments of an air", which Clarke fashioned into this tune.
ye-banks-and-braes.source: William Stenhouse, Illustrations of the Lyric Poetry and Music of Scotland (Edinburgh: Blackwood, 1853), pp. 346 and 347, quoting Burns's letter to George Thomson of November 1794, read from the scan

skye-boat-song.text: Half the tune came from Hebridean rowers and half from the book's editor: "Four bars taken down from Hebridean boatmen, four bars added by A. C. Macleod."
skye-boat-song.source: an undated Cramer reprint of Songs of the North, vol. I, ed. A. C. Macleod and Harold Boulton, No. V, p. 18, read from the scan

skye-boat-song.text: J. S. Blackie's Scottish Song (1889) printed the line "Thunder-clouds rend the air". Our National Songs (Cramer, 1923) has "Thunderclaps", as it is sung today, and so does an undated reprint of Songs of the North.
skye-boat-song.source: J. S. Blackie, Scottish Song (Edinburgh: Blackwood, 1889), p. 239; Our National Songs, ed. Harold Boulton (London: Cramer, 1923), No. 10; an undated Cramer reprint of Songs of the North, vol. I, No. V; read from the scans

praise-to-the-lord.text: The German hymn, Lobe den Herren, was the favourite of King Friedrich Wilhelm III of Prussia. The writer Lauxmann relates how he was affected by hearing it sung in a boat in the mines at Waldenburg in 1800.
praise-to-the-lord.source: John Julian, A Dictionary of Hymnology (1907), vol. 1, p. 683, "Lobe den Herren", citing Lauxmann, read from the scan

praise-to-the-lord.text: With this hymn the Prussian War Minister, Albrecht von Roon, celebrated his jubilee of service, near Paris, on January 9, 1871.
praise-to-the-lord.source: John Julian, A Dictionary of Hymnology (1907), vol. 1, p. 683, "Lobe den Herren", read from the scan

come-ye-thankful-people.text: Henry Alford complained in 1865 that his hymn had been "much disfigured by alterations made without the author's consent", and said he was "responsible for this form of it only".
come-ye-thankful-people.source: Henry Alford, The Poetical Works of Henry Alford (London, 1865), p. 300, footnote, read from the scan

come-ye-thankful-people.text: Alford changed his lines "From His field shall purge away / All that doth offend that day" at the request of the Tract Committee of the Christian Knowledge Society, "as possibly bearing an ambiguous meaning".
come-ye-thankful-people.source: Henry Alford, The Poetical Works of Henry Alford (London, 1865), p. 301, footnote, read from the scan

now-thank-we-all-our-god.text: Catherine Winkworth titled her translation "The Chorus of God's Thankful Children".
now-thank-we-all-our-god.source: Lyra Germanica, second series: The Christian Life, tr. Catherine Winkworth (London: Longman, 1858), p. 145, read from the scan

now-thank-we-all-our-god.text: The editors of The English Hymnal complained: "It is distressing to hear 'Nun Danket' or 'St. Anne' raced through at about twice the proper speed." They marked this hymn "Very slow and majestic".
now-thank-we-all-our-god.source: The English Hymnal (1906 edition), preface and Hymn 533, read from the scan

we-gather-together.text: In 1626 Adrianus Valerius printed the Dutch words to an older tune, "Hey wilder dan wild" ("Hey, wilder than wild"), with lute tablature underneath.
we-gather-together.source: Adrianus Valerius, Nederlandtsche Gedenck-clanck (Haarlem, 1626), p. 170, read from the scan

we-gather-together.text: A 1928 American hymnal told congregations to sing the first two verses in unison, men and women taking turns if they liked, and only the last "in full harmony".
we-gather-together.source: The Abingdon Hymnal, ed. Earl Enyeart Harper (New York: Abingdon Press, 1928), No. 207, footnote, read from the scan

i-will-bow-and-be-simple.text: In Mary Hazzard's songbook it has no title and is signed only "North Family", with no village, giver or date.
i-will-bow-and-be-simple.source: Mary Hazzard's manuscript songbook, Winterthur Library, ASC 893, page 108

i-will-bow-and-be-simple.text: The songbook calls itself "A Collection of Extra Songs of Various Kinds Written and Pricked For the Purpose of Retaining them". This song comes in it between songs dated 1851 and 1852.
i-will-bow-and-be-simple.source: Mary Hazzard's manuscript songbook, Winterthur Library, ASC 893, title page and pages 105, 108 and 116

o-the-beautiful-treasure.text: In Mary Hazzard's songbook it is headed "Valuable Riches" and signed "Holy Ground", with no giver or date.
o-the-beautiful-treasure.source: Mary Hazzard's manuscript songbook, Winterthur Library, ASC 893, page 70

o-the-beautiful-treasure.text: Two pages on in the same songbook comes "Elder Joseph Brackett's Song March 1849".
o-the-beautiful-treasure.source: Mary Hazzard's manuscript songbook, Winterthur Library, ASC 893, pages 70 and 72

who-will-bow-and-bend.text: In Mary Hazzard's songbook it has no title, place, giver or date. Two songs away on each side are songs signed by Canterbury's Second Family, dated "Feb 22nd 1847" and "April 1847".
who-will-bow-and-bend.source: Mary Hazzard's manuscript songbook, Winterthur Library, ASC 893, pages 16 to 20

who-will-bow-and-bend.text: Mary Hazzard's songbook writes "Who will turn and twist and real". We sing "reel".
who-will-bow-and-bend.source: Mary Hazzard's manuscript songbook, Winterthur Library, ASC 893, page 18

heavenly-treasures.text: In Mary Hazzard's songbook it has no title, only the line "Sung by Jack thro Abram P. on the holy Mount Aug 30th".
heavenly-treasures.source: Mary Hazzard's manuscript songbook, Winterthur Library, ASC 893, page 23

heavenly-treasures.text: Its year comes from the song above it on the same page: "August 30th 1847. Sung by the Savior on the Holy Mount thro Abm Perkins".
heavenly-treasures.source: Mary Hazzard's manuscript songbook, Winterthur Library, ASC 893, page 23

las-mananitas.text: In his memoirs of 1904 the geographer Antonio García Cubas tells of riding by moonlight up to the plain of Atotonilco el Grande. Outside a house there, as day came near, they began "cantar alegremente las mañanitas", "Despierta, mi bien despierta", and soon the windows opened.
las-mananitas.source: Antonio García Cubas, El libro de mis recuerdos (Mexico City, 1904), p. 547, read from the scan

las-mananitas.text: In 1929 Anita Brenner wrote of the Guadalupe fiesta: "Serenade the madonna with the mañanitas", the "prerogative of the Mother, and prerogative, too, of sweethearts and budding maidens on birthday mornings."
las-mananitas.source: Anita Brenner, Idols Behind Altars (New York: Harcourt, Brace, 1929), p. 153, read from the scan

riu-riu-chiu.text: It comes from a book of villancicos printed in Venice in 1556. Rafael Mitjana came across it in Uppsala University's library and believed it the only known copy.
