riu-riu-chiu.source: Rafael Mitjana, Cincuenta y cuatro canciones españolas del siglo XVI (Uppsala, 1909), introduction ("un ejemplar probablemente único"); Mitjana in Lavignac, Encyclopédie de la musique, part I, vol. 4 (Paris, 1920), p. 2006 ("que nous croyons unique exemplaire connu"); read from the scans

riu-riu-chiu.text: In the 1556 print the bass sings the refrain alone first, then all four voices sing it, and the verses are the bass's alone: "solo las coblas".
riu-riu-chiu.source: Villancicos de diversos autores (Venice: Girolamo Scotto, 1556), Uppsala University Library, fols. 42v to 43r, read from the library's photograph on Wikimedia Commons

noche-de-paz.text: The earliest known printing of these Spanish words is in El Himnario evangélico, a New York hymnal of 1893. It calls the tune by an English name, "Holy Night", and names no one: not Gruber, not Mohr, and not whoever wrote "¡Noche de paz, noche de amor! Todo duerme en derredor."
noche-de-paz.source: El Himnario evangélico, para el uso de todas las iglesias (New York: Sociedad Americana de Tratados, copyright 1893), No. 48, p. 38, read from the scan

noche-de-paz.text: In 1893 the second verse's second line was "En el campo al pastor", and so it stayed in Spanish hymnals of 1894 and 1907. The earliest printing we have found of the line as "Oye humilde el fiel pastor" is in El Nuevo himnario evangélico (New York, 1915).
noche-de-paz.source: El Himnario evangélico (New York, 1893), No. 48, p. 38; Himnos evangélicos (New York, 1894), No. 48, p. 24; Himnario provisional, ed. James H. Van Buren (Philadelphia, 1907), No. 18; El Nuevo himnario evangélico (New York: Sociedad Americana de Tratados, copyright 1915), No. 83, p. 32; read from the scans

pastores-a-belen.text: The 1916 New Mexico songbook this version comes from says it at last brings out the music of the "Cánticos espirituales, recogidos por el P. Ralliere". Words and music, it admits, don't always keep the rules of the art, but the people of its region "así los conoce, así los canta, así los quiere" (knows them, sings them, loves them this way), so it left them "intactos" as far as it could.
pastores-a-belen.source: Cánticos espirituales con música, recogidos por la "Revista Católica" (Las Vegas, New Mexico, 1916), the note "¡¡¡IMPORTANTE!!!" (leaf 9), read from the scan

pastores-a-belen.text: Father J. B. Ralliere, who collected the Cánticos espirituales, was brought from France and served Tomé, New Mexico, from 1858 to 1911. When he died in July 1915 he was buried beneath the church floor.
pastores-a-belen.source: Florence Hawley Ellis, "Tomé and Father J. B. R.", New Mexico Historical Review 30, no. 2 (April 1955), p. 103, and no. 3 (July 1955), pp. 217 and 218; Cánticos espirituales con música (Las Vegas, New Mexico, 1916), the note "¡¡¡IMPORTANTE!!!" (leaf 9); read from the scans

el-cant-dels-ocells.text: Introducing it in a lecture printed in 1917, Lluís Millet said it "té una de les melodíes més hermoses de la terra catalana" (has one of the most beautiful melodies of the Catalan land): "La modalitat bon xic oriental que la caracteritza, li dóna una idealitat melangiosa que enamora" (its somewhat Eastern mode gives it a melancholy, enchanting ideal beauty). His harmony for men's voices, he said, he had written "ja fa uns quants anys" (some years ago).
el-cant-dels-ocells.source: Lluís Millet, Pel nostre ideal (Barcelona, 1917), p. 209, read from the scan

el-cant-dels-ocells.text: Francesc Pujol, in the Materials of the Obra del Cançoner Popular de Catalunya (vol. I, fascicle II, printed 1928), calls it "L'un des plus beaux noëls de notre chansonnier" (one of the finest carols in our songbook), and says: "Ce délicieux noël n'est autre chose que la chanson antérieure, «Les contrebandiers», véritablement transfigurée" (this delightful carol is nothing other than the song before it, The Smugglers, truly transfigured).
el-cant-dels-ocells.source: Obra del Cançoner Popular de Catalunya, Materials, vol. I, fascicle II (Barcelona, 1928; the volume's title page says 1926), p. 380 (p. 284 of Francesc Pujol's French section), read from the scan

oyfn-pripetchik.text: Mark Warshawsky's own songbook, printed in Warsaw in 1901 with a foreword by Sholem Aleichem, has it as "Der alef-beys".
oyfn-pripetchik.source: M. M. Warshawsky, Yidishe folkslider (Warsaw: Aleksander Gins, 1901), title page and p. 13, read from the scan

oyfn-pripetchik.text: Susman Kisselgof's songbook "for the Jewish school and family" printed it among its secular folk songs, for three voices and piano, arranged by Pesach Lvov.
oyfn-pripetchik.source: Z. Kisselgof, Lider-zamelbukh far der yidisher shul un familye, 4th edition (Berlin: Juval), music part p. 19, No. 13, read from the scan

rozhinkes-mit-mandlen.text: Its melody was already in a New York piano arrangement from Goldfaden's Shulamith, Simon Adler's "Raisines & Almonds", printed "Copyright 1890", eighteen years before Goldfaden died.
rozhinkes-mit-mandlen.source: Simon Adler, Sulamitha, Op. 46 (New York: Theodor Lohr, 1890), cover and p. 2, read from the scan (Brown Digital Repository bdr:100759)

rozhinkes-mit-mandlen.text: New York sheet music sold it in Yiddish and English, "Raisins and Almonds", "From The Opera 'Shulamith'", with Goldfaden's portrait on the cover.
rozhinkes-mit-mandlen.source: "Raisins and Almonds", arr. A. R. Zagler (New York: S. Schenker, about 1910 to 1917), cover, read from the scan (Brown Digital Repository bdr:100085)

the-first-noel.text: Did the carol once sing of "three poor shepherds"? Davies Gilbert's words of 1823, its earliest known printing, already say "certain poor Shepherds". William Sandys's book of 1833 has "three" in its words, but "certain" under its printed tune.
the-first-noel.source: Davies Gilbert, Some Ancient Christmas Carols, second edition (London, 1823), Carol IX, p. 28; William Sandys, Christmas Carols, Ancient and Modern (London, 1833), pp. 74 and 75 and the air "The First Nowell"; read from the scans

the-first-noel.text: The tune is one eight-bar phrase sung three times over, closing on the third note of the scale rather than the home note. In 1915 Annie Gilchrist suggested it began as a treble part sung above an old hymn tune.
the-first-noel.source: Annie G. Gilchrist, "Note on the Carol 'The First Nowell'", Journal of the Folk-Song Society, vol. 5, no. 19 (London, 1915), pp. 240 to 242, read from the scan

o-little-town-of-bethlehem.text: Lewis Redner wrote that Phillips Brooks asked him on a Friday, "Redner, have you ground out that music yet?" Late that Saturday night he woke "hearing an angel-strain whispering in my ear", jotted down the tune, and added the harmony on Sunday morning.
o-little-town-of-bethlehem.source: Louis F. Benson, Studies of Familiar Hymns (Philadelphia: Westminster Press, 1903), pp. 4 to 6, Lewis H. Redner's written statement, read from the scan

o-little-town-of-bethlehem.text: Some British and Irish hymnals set it to FOREST GREEN, a folk tune Ralph Vaughan Williams noted in December 1903 from Mr. Garman at Forest Green, Surrey. The Folk-Song Society's journal printed it in 1906 as "The Ploughboy's Dream".
o-little-town-of-bethlehem.source: Journal of the Folk-Song Society, vol. 2, No. 8 (London, 1906), pp. 203 and 204, No. 48, "The Ploughboy's Dream", read from the scan; Hymnary.org, Church Hymnary, 4th edition (2005), No. 304, FOREST GREEN

angels-we-have-heard-on-high.text: The Holy Family Hymns of 1860, where James Chadwick's English began, marks the verse "Solo" and the Gloria "Chorus". Its preface explains: a few singers who know the tune sing the verse, and the whole congregation answers.
angels-we-have-heard-on-high.source: The Holy Family Hymns, with Music for the Holy Family Hymns (London: Richardson and Son, 1860), preface, p. viii, and music, pp. 8 and 9, read from the scan

angels-we-have-heard-on-high.text: In the Latin Bible, Luke's angels sing "Gloria in altissimis Deo". The carol's "in excelsis" comes from the Gloria of the Mass, the ancient hymn that opens with the angels' song in those words.
angels-we-have-heard-on-high.source: Latin Vulgate, Luke 2:14, at DRBO.org; Adrian Fortescue, "Gloria in Excelsis Deo", The Catholic Encyclopedia, vol. 6 (New York: Robert Appleton Company, 1909)

good-king-wenceslas.text: John Mason Neale first told it in prose, in Deeds of Faith, a children's book with a preface dated 1849. In that tale it is Advent, and the servant Otto finds the king's footprints glowing "as with a holy fire".
good-king-wenceslas.source: J. M. Neale, Deeds of Faith: Stories for Children from Church History, second edition (London: J. and C. Mozley, and Masters and Co., 1860), Preface and No. XI, "The Legend of S. Wenceslaus", pp. 129 to 135

good-king-wenceslas.text: In the carol book H. R. Bramley and John Stainer edited, the verses are shared out by speaker: the king's words go to a solo tenor, the page's to a solo treble, and the story told around them to the chorus.
good-king-wenceslas.source: H. R. Bramley and John Stainer, Christmas Carols New and Old, first series (London: Novello, Ewer and Co.; a printing of the 1870s), No. X, "Good King Wenceslas", pp. 20 and 21, read from the scan

the-holly-and-the-ivy.text: Cecil Sharp filled out Mary Clayton's words from Mrs. Wyatt of East Harptree. He changed one line: for her verse 2 ending, "On Christmas day in the morn", which he called "obviously incorrect", he printed the broadsides' "To be our sweet Saviour".
the-holly-and-the-ivy.source: Cecil J. Sharp, English Folk-Carols (London: Novello and Co., 1911), No. VII, pp. 17 and 18, and Notes, No. 7, pp. 63 and 64; New York Public Library copy, read from the scan

the-holly-and-the-ivy.text: Why a "merry" organ? William Henry Husk noted that Chaucer gave the church organ the same word: in the Canterbury Tales, the rooster Chanticleer's voice was "merrier than the merry organ / On mass days that in the church goon".
the-holly-and-the-ivy.source: William Henry Husk (editor), Songs of the Nativity (London: John Camden Hotten, undated), "The Holly and the Ivy", Husk's note, p. 84; University of California Libraries copy, read from the scan's text

we-three-kings.text: Hopkins's own printing gives each king his own staff, headed Gaspard, Melchior and Balthazar. A note at its foot says: "Men's voices are best for the parts of the Three Kings, but the music is set in the G clef for the accommodation of children".
we-three-kings.source: John H. Hopkins, Jr., Carols, Hymns, and Songs (New York: Church Book Depository, undated, catalogued as [1863?]), "Three Kings of Orient", pp. 12 and 13; Princeton Theological Seminary Library, Benson Collection, read from the scan

we-three-kings.text: The "Hallelujah" you sing in the last verse is the word of Hopkins's earliest printing we have seen. His own second edition, of 1872, changed it to "Alleluia", and his third, of 1882, kept the change.
we-three-kings.source: John H. Hopkins, Jr., Carols, Hymns, and Songs (New York: Church Book Depository, [1863?]), pp. 12 and 13; second edition, enlarged (New York: Church Book Depository and E. P. Dutton and Co., preface dated November 1872), pp. 12 and 13; third edition (New York: E. and J. B. Young and Co., 1882), pp. 18 and 19; Princeton Theological Seminary Library, Benson Collection, read from the scans

it-came-upon-the-midnight-clear.text: The tune began in 1850 as Study No. 23, a choir-practice piece in Richard Storrs Willis's Church Chorals and Choir Studies, set to Philip Doddridge's "See Israel's gentle shepherd stand". It held only about the first half of CAROL, the tune we sing.
it-came-upon-the-midnight-clear.source: R. Storrs Willis, Church Chorals and Choir Studies (New York: Clark, Austin and Smith, 1850), Study No. 23, p. 93; Princeton Theological Seminary Library copy, read from the scan; Hymnology Archive, "It Came Upon the Midnight Clear"

it-came-upon-the-midnight-clear.text: John H. Morison, the editor who received the carol in 1849, later wrote that however poor his own Christmas sermon might be, "the reading and singing of this hymn are enough to make up for all deficiencies".
it-came-upon-the-midnight-clear.source: Alfred P. Putnam, Singers and Songs of the Liberal Faith (Boston: Roberts Brothers, 1875), "Edmund Hamilton Sears", p. 308, Morison's letter; Princeton Theological Seminary Library copy, read from the scan

in-the-bleak-midwinter.text: Scribner's Monthly teased the poem a month early. Its December 1871 "Old Cabinet" column spoke of "a little poem" in the writer's breast-pocket, "sweet and clear and musical", that celebrates the first Christmas morning "In the bleak mid-winter / Long ago."
in-the-bleak-midwinter.source: Scribner's Monthly, vol. 3, no. 2 (New York: Scribner and Co., December 1871), "The Old Cabinet", p. 239; Brigham Young University, Harold B. Lee Library copy, read from the scan

in-the-bleak-midwinter.text: The English Hymnal of 1906 prints Holst's music for Rossetti's first verse only. Its note calls the metre "peculiar" and says the music "can easily be adapted to the others", and an extra line shows how verses 2 and 3 run.
in-the-bleak-midwinter.source: The English Hymnal, with Tunes (London: Henry Frowde, Oxford University Press; first edition, preface dated Ascension Day 1906), No. 25, CRANHAM, p. 44; Graduate Theological Union copy, read from the scan

coventry-carol.text: In verse 1, Sharp's printed words and his treble part have "O sisters too", but his tenor and bass parts spell it "two": the mother may be speaking to the two other women on stage with her.
coventry-carol.source: Thomas Sharp, A Dissertation on the Pageants or Dramatic Mysteries Anciently Performed at Coventry (Coventry: Merridew and Son, 1825), p. 113 and the plates numbered 116 and 117; copy digitized by Google, holding library not named, read from the scan

coventry-carol.text: In the 1591 setting, every "lullay" that ends the refrain, verse 1 or verse 3 closes on a major chord in this minor-key song, the treble on B natural, not B-flat. Verse 2 alone ends on a bare open chord, with no third.
coventry-carol.source: Thomas Sharp, A Dissertation on the Pageants or Dramatic Mysteries Anciently Performed at Coventry (Coventry: Merridew and Son, 1825), "Song II" on the plates numbered 116 and 117 (treble, tenor and bass); copy digitized by Google, holding library not named, read from the scan

what-child-is-this.text: Some hymnals say Dix made this carol from a longer poem of his, "The Manger Throne", of 1865. But "The Manger Throne" is a different carol by Dix, beginning "Like silver lamps in a distant shrine", printed twelve numbers earlier in the same carol book.
what-child-is-this.source: H. R. Bramley and John Stainer, Christmas Carols New and Old, first series (London: Novello, Ewer and Co., undated printing, catalogued [187?]), No. II, "The Manger Throne", p. 4, No. XIV, "What Child is this?", pp. 32 and 33, and the first series' index; University of California Libraries copy, read from the scan; and The Canterbury Dictionary of Hymnology (2013), "What child is this, who laid to rest"

what-child-is-this.text: The book's tune, in E minor, bends with its direction. Coming down, on "this" in the first line and the second "this" of the chorus, it has C natural; climbing back to the home note, at "watch" and "Son of", C sharp and D sharp.
what-child-is-this.source: H. R. Bramley and John Stainer, Christmas Carols New and Old, first series (London: Novello, Ewer and Co., undated printing, catalogued [187?]), No. XIV, "What Child is this?", pp. 32 and 33; University of California Libraries copy, read from the scan

o-come-o-come-emmanuel.text: The Revised Edition of Hymns Ancient and Modern prints "To be sung in Unison" over this hymn. Each verse starts mf, it drops to p for "That mourns in lonely exile here", and every refrain is marked ff.
o-come-o-come-emmanuel.source: Hymns Ancient and Modern for Use in the Services of the Church, with Accompanying Tunes, Revised Edition (London: printed for the proprietors by William Clowes and Sons, Limited; undated later printing, catalogued 1874), Hymn 49, pp. 34 and 35; Harold B. Lee Library, Brigham Young University, read from the scan

o-come-o-come-emmanuel.text: The refrain's promise has changed tense. The Latin of 1710 and Neale's English of 1851 say Emmanuel "is born"; the Hymnal Noted, dated 1856, sings "Shall be born", and Hymns Ancient and Modern "Shall come".
o-come-o-come-emmanuel.source: Psalteriolum Cantionum Catholicarum (Cologne, 1710), p. 269, page image in Hymnology Archive, Fig. 4b; J. M. Neale, Mediaeval Hymns and Sequences (London: Joseph Masters, 1851), p. 119; The Hymnal Noted, Part II (London and New York: Novello, Ewer and Co., and J. Masters; title page dated 1856, a later printing), No. 65 (or 30), p. 131; Hymns Ancient and Modern (London: Novello and Co., preface dated Lent, 1861), Hymn 36; read from the scans

i-saw-three-ships.text: William Sandys, who printed an early form of this tune in 1833, wrote that it was "very similar to one of the old Shakspearian tunes", There Lived a Man in Babylon.
i-saw-three-ships.source: William Sandys, Christmas Carols, Ancient and Modern (London: Richard Beckley, 1833), notes on the airs, p. 187, on air No. 9; University of California Libraries copy, read from the scan

i-saw-three-ships.text: The six-eight tune we sing is in William Henry Husk's Songs of the Nativity of 1868, note for note, a tone higher. The air Sandys printed in 1833 is the same melody in three-four time, with the same notes but one.
i-saw-three-ships.source: William Henry Husk (editor), Songs of the Nativity (London: John Camden Hotten, undated), "On Christmas Day in the Morning", p. 190; William Sandys, Christmas Carols, Ancient and Modern (London: Richard Beckley, 1833), air No. 9; both University of California Libraries copies; compared note by note with H. R. Bramley and John Stainer, Christmas Carols New and Old, complete edition, No. 64, p. 164; read from the scans
